newsitem.title: UK: Labour's Brown ducks out of TV debate - UK Lib Dems.
newsitem.headline: Labour's Brown ducks out of TV debate - UK Lib Dems.

text.p: Labour economics spokesman Gordon Brown was accused by the Liberal Democrats on Friday of having ducked out of a television election debate on economic policy.
The minority party, furious at repeated charges by Brown that their tax and spending plans do not add up, claimed he was avoiding opportunities to defend his own manifesto pledges.

Christopher Huhne, a Liberal economic adviser, said the main parties had agreed to a debate on next Sunday's BBC On the Record programme between Brown, Chancellor Kenneth Clarke and Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesman Malcolm Bruce.
But Huhne, a City of London economist, told reporters Labour had now said it would put up its Trade and Industry spokeswoman, Margaret Beckett, instead.

"They don't want to be challenged. If Margaret Beckett falls flat on her face, she is not the party spokesman on treasury matters. They can say she couldn't be expected to know the detail," Huhne said.

A BBC spokeswoman said Brown had been asked to appear on the programme, but added he had never definitely said "Yes". "He was invited but it was never confirmed," she said. A Labour spokesman pointed out that Brown had already appeared in one TV debate with Clarke and Bruce, and said he could not therefore be accused of avoiding debate.
Brown has used the last two daily Labour news conferences to attack the Liberals for "completely uncosted" spending pledges.

But on Friday, Bruce hit back, saying Liberal plans, to be paid for by a 1p rise in the standard rate of income tax, a higher rate tax band and higher cigarette duty, were "given a clean bill of health" by the independent Institute for Fiscal Studies.
"I have no alternative but to interpret this as another example of U.S.-style attack' negative campaigning regardless of the truth of the allegations," he told Brown.
"I regard this behaviour as particularly reprehensible since you are now avoiding previously arranged opportunities to defend your own uncosted policies," he wrote in an open letter.

Huhne said Brown's own plans were hard to defend since they, like those of the Conservatives, implied a 0.4 percent annual growth of public spending in real terms over the next three years, half the rate of growth delivered by any parliament in any government since 1945.
He said Liberal plans, implying one percent real growth, were "at least in the realm of the real world". -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7767
